question: A 22-year-old woman presents to her physician with an increased vaginal discharge. She has no other complaints. She has recently changed her sexual partner, who claims to have no genitourinary symptoms. They do not use condoms. Her vital signs are as follows: blood pressure, 110/80 mm Hg; heart rate, 65/min; respiratory rate, 11/min; and temperature, 36.6℃ (97.9℉). Her physical examination is unremarkable. The gynecologic examination shows increased production of a white-yellow vaginal discharge. Wet mount microscopy shows the below picture. Which of the following treatments is indicated in this patient?

options.opd: No treatment required in the patient with minor symptoms

analysis: The patient's presentation of increased vaginal discharge, particularly with a white-yellow discharge and the context of a recent change in sexual partner, suggests a possible diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis (BV) or a sexually transmitted infection (STI). The wet mount microscopy likely shows clue cells, which are indicative of BV. The first-line treatment for bacterial vaginosis is metronidazole, which can be administered orally. Clindamycin is also effective but is typically used in cases where metronidazole is contraindicated or not tolerated. Given the symptoms and the likely diagnosis, peroral metronidazole is the most appropriate treatment option.
